It's one of the fastest-growing products in AI: 13 million monthly active users, 20X growth this year, and more tokens processed daily than all of OpenRouter. But the overnight success took 16 years, one legal entity, and nine YC applications.

Everything begins with finding some issues in a great closed-source product and building a great community around something that not only solves these issues but also benefits from all the advantages of Open-Source. Most of the founders I talked to started like that.

To lay a foundation and carve out a distinct identity, these startups initially position themselves as “THE Open-Source counterpart to X.” This strategy serves as a tactical entry point, helping them target a niche market segment and establish brand recall. [...] A testament to this is Supabase, which even amidst its success, continues to call itself the “Open-Source Firebase alternative” — a name so iconic that it simplifies Supabase’s proposition into an easily digestible pitch. Indeed, it’s when they revamped their branding with this tagline that they exploded on platforms like HackerNews and the number of users went from a dozen to 800+ in 3 days (don’t hesitate to listen to one of the founders explaining the underlying in this podcast). [...] ⚠️ But you have to know, that building an Open-Source company is hard. And maybe harder than a classic SaaS business. results.title: Linux Foundation Launches OpenTofu: A New Open Source Alternative to Terraform
results.content:
“We believe that the essential building blocks of the modern Internet—tools such as Linux, Kubernetes, and Terraform—must be truly open source," said Yevgeniy (Jim) Brikman, Co-founder and CEO of Gruntwork, and OpenTofu founding team member. "That is the only way to ensure that we are building our industry on top of solid and predictable underpinnings. That is why we are so happy that OpenTofu is now a part of the Linux Foundation: having this project in the hands of a foundation, rather than a single company, means OpenTofu will be community-driven and truly open source—always.” [...] BILBAO, SPAIN – September 20, 2023 – Today, the Linux Foundation announced the formation of OpenTofu, an open source alternative to Terraform's widely used infrastructure as code provisioning tool. Previously named OpenTF, OpenTofu is an open and community-driven response to Terraform's recently announced license change from a Mozilla Public License v2.0 (MPLv2) to a Business Source License v1.1, providing everyone with a reliable, open source alternative under a neutral governance model. [...] "The OpenTofu initiative will be driven exclusively by the pursuit of the community’s vision and will work for the community’s needs — not the interests of any individual company."

-Marcin Wyszynski, Core OpenTofu Contributor, CPO at Spacelift

"With OpenTofu, our goal is to create a stable foundation for the open-sourced future of Terraform. The community response to the project was humbling, and going forward our plan is simple - listen, learn, internalize, prioritize, execute, rinse and repeat."

- Omry Hay, Core OpenTofu Contributor, CTO at env0

"OpenTofu will be everything legacy Terraform should have been: community-first and impartial.

- Sebastian Stadil, Core OpenTofu Contributor, Founder of Scalr

results.content:
Comment "OPEN" to get this website with free and opensource alternatives to popular paid apps.   
  
If you are still paying for tools and subscriptions, then you are literally wasting your money.  
  
There's a website that fixes this called OpenAlternative.  
  
It's a directory of free and open-source alternatives to almost every paid tool you use.  
  
And here's the fun part.  
  
The website itself is open source too.  
  
So the tool that finds you free alternatives is also completely free to use.  
  
You can search for tools like Slack, Notion, Figma, Photoshop, or Canva.  
  
And instantly see a list of open-source replacements for each one.  
  
Every listing shows you the GitHub star count, the license type, and how active the community is. [...] So you're not just picking a random tool, you're picking one people actually use and maintain.  
  
It started as one developer manually collecting 70 tools on a weekend.  
  
Now it's grown into one of the biggest open-source directories on the internet.  
  
Whatever software you're paying for right now, there's a good chance someone already built a free version.
